==Problem==

Which of these numbers is less than its reciprocal?

<imath>\text{(A)}\ {-2} \qquad \text{(B)}\ {-1} \qquad \text{(C)}\ 0 \qquad \text{(D)}\ 1 \qquad \text{(E)}\ 2</imath>

==Solution 1==

The reciprocal of <imath>-2</imath> is <imath>-\frac{1}{2}</imath>.  Since <imath>-2 < -\frac{1}{2}</imath>, <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A)}\ {-2}}</imath> is correct.

The reciprocal of <imath>-1</imath> is <imath>-1</imath>.  Since <imath>-1 = -1</imath>, (B) is incorrect.

The reciprocal of <imath>0</imath> is undefined, so (C) is incorrect.

The reciprocal of <imath>1</imath> is <imath>1</imath>.  Since <imath>1 = 1</imath>, (D) is incorrect.

The reciprocal of <imath>2</imath> is <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath>.  Since <imath>2 > \frac{1}{2}</imath>, (E) is incorrect.

==Solution 2==

Let <imath>x</imath> be a real number that is less than its reciprocal, that is, <imath>x < \frac{1}{x}</imath>.

Since <imath>\frac{1}{x}</imath> must be defined, <imath>x \neq 0</imath>.

If <imath>x</imath> is positive, then <imath>x^2 < 1</imath>, so <imath>0 < x < 1</imath>.

If <imath>x</imath> is negative, then <imath>x^2 > 1</imath>, so <imath>x < -1</imath>.

Therefore, <imath>x < \frac{1}{x}</imath> if and only if either <imath>x < -1</imath> or <imath>0 < x < 1</imath>.  Of the answer choices, only <imath>\boxed {\textbf{(A)}\ {-2}}</imath> is a possible value of <imath>x</imath>.

==Solution 3==

Starting again with <imath>x < \frac{1}{x}</imath>, we avoid multiplication by <imath>x</imath>.   Instead, move everything to the left, and find a common denominator:

<imath>x < \frac{1}{x}</imath>

<imath>x - \frac{1}{x} < 0</imath>

<imath>\frac{x^2 - 1}{x} < 0</imath>

<imath>\frac{(x+1)(x-1)}{x} < 0</imath>

Divide this expression at <imath>x=-1</imath>, <imath>x=0</imath>, and <imath>x=1</imath>, as those are the three points where the expression on the left will "change sign".

If <imath>x<-1</imath>, all three of those terms will be negative, and the inequality is true.  Therefore, <imath>(-\infty, -1)</imath> is part of our solution set.

If <imath>-1 < x < 0</imath>, the <imath>(x+1)</imath> term will become positive, but the other two terms remain negative.  Thus, there are no solutions in this region.

If <imath>0 < x < 1</imath>, then both <imath>(x+1)</imath> and <imath>x</imath> are positive, while <imath>(x-1)</imath> remains negative.  Thus, the entire region <imath>(0, 1)</imath> is part of the solution set.

If <imath>1 < x</imath>, then all three terms are positive, and there are no solutions.

At all three "boundary points", the function is either <imath>0</imath> or undefined.  Therefore, the entire solution set is <imath>(-\infty, -1) \cup (0, 1)</imath>, and the only option in that region is <imath>x=-2</imath>, leading to <imath>\boxed{A}</imath>.
